characterization_methods.key_findings: Hardness after aging at 625 °C for 1 h = 852.8 ± 24.6 HV; this is the lowest value in the 625 °C plateau (which stabilizes around 888 HV at 3–10 h).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Load 9.8 N for 15 s; average of 5 measurements; electrolytically polished sample (10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol)
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the Vickers hardness of the 15Al alloy after aging at 625 °C for 1 h.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.key_findings: At 625 °C/1 h the 15Al alloy shows an essentially fully transformed β-Mn matrix with fine 'New precipitates'; the α→β-Mn transformation is essentially complete at these higher temperatures.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Electrolytically polished surface; main field 50 μm scale bar with 10 μm inset
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize the microstructure of the 15Al alloy after aging at 625 °C for 1 h (Fig. 7 contains a 625 °C–1 h panel).

interfaces.interface_notes: The fine BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates form at the interfaces between the β-Mn; the increase in Al content decreases the content of the FCC Cu-rich phase between the β-Mn interfaces. For the 15Al alloy the Cu-rich FCC particles were confirmed by TEM/SAED at the β-Mn interfaces.
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Raw materials of high purity (>99.9%) melted under an argon atmosphere to produce ingots of nominal composition Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu (at.%).
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm^3 samples for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching.
The solution-treated sample was aged at 625 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. This is the terminal state of the specified sample.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and the value given by the average of 5 measurements.

fine particles / new precipitates within the β-Mn (and at β-Mn interfaces)

precipitates.distribution: fine particles distributed within the β-Mn

structures.overall_structure: After aging the 15Al alloy at 625 °C for 1 h, the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn (since at 600 °C and above the α matrix almost completely transformed into β-Mn within just 1 h), with abundant fine BCC and FCC precipitates distributed within the β-Mn.

unmapped_findings: 15Al alloy (Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu, at.%) EDS-measured chemical composition (Table 1): Fe 44.6, Mn 35.2, Al 15.0, Cu 5.2 at.% (source b0012/b0013).

For the 15Al alloy, the optimal aging temperature range for achieving ultra-high hardness was mainly 525 °C–600 °C, and increasing Al content shifted this optimal range to higher temperatures (b0038).
For the 15Al alloy aged at 625 °C and 650 °C the hardness stabilized between 800 HV and 900 HV with prolonged aging time; the 625 °C series plateau is near ~888 HV (b0037).

The paper's fracture-toughness (KIC), nanoindentation and TEM results were obtained on the peak-hardness 15Al condition (600 °C/6 h, 965.6 HV), not on the 625 °C/1 h sample; hence KIC (8.6 MPa·m^1/2), nanoindentation hardness (11.7 ± 0.4 GPa) and intrinsic β-Mn hardness (12.1 ± 0.3 GPa) are not assigned to this sample (b0021, b0060, b0061).

β-Mn in the hardest 15Al sample had a composition of Mn 36.8 at.%, Al 14.3 at.%, Cu 2.8 at.%; increase of Al raised the Al dissolved in β-Mn and slightly enhanced its intrinsic hardness (b0060, b0067).
